title: Africa's missing states, 430–1911
summary: Many African states are missing from the border data, which draws mostly the large empires and the colonial powers. This layer adds them: the Berber kingdoms of late-Roman Mauretania and the Aurès; the Wolof states of Senegambia, the Fula imamates, Kaabu and the Moorish emirates; Kong, the Mossi kingdoms, Dagbon, Denkyira, Akwamu, Dahomey and Benin; the Hausa kingdoms, Nupe, Kebbi, Agadez, Damagaram and Baguirmi; the Ethiopian, Gibe and Somali sultanates and kingdoms, the Shilluk, Kilwa and Pate; Buganda, Bunyoro, Rwanda and Burundi; Loango, Ndongo, Matamba, Kasanje, Kuba, Luba, Lunda and Kazembe; Mapungubwe, Great Zimbabwe, Mutapa, Butua and the Rozvi; and Maravi, Gaza, the Nguni and Sotho kingdoms, the Lozi and the Sakalava. Dates and rulers come from cited reference articles. Few pre-colonial African frontiers were ever surveyed or described, and many of these states ruled people and trade routes more than fixed territory, so every outline here is an approximate, deliberately conservative reconstruction of each state's core lands, not its full sphere of tribute.

regions.name: Jolof Empire
regions.note: The Wolof confederation of Jolof, Waalo, Kajoor (Cayor), Bawol (Baol), Sine and Saloum under the Burba of Jolof, formed c. 1360. Civil wars (1455–1489) weakened it; Koli Tenguella took Futa Toro from it in 1513 and Sine and Saloum broke away in 1520. Only the constituent states are drawn; Takrur, Bambuk and the Gambia chiefdoms that paid tribute at its height are left out. Pre-colonial frontiers here are approximate, and the founding date is traditional. Sources: Wikipedia 'Jolof Empire'; frontiers of the constituent states follow the CC0 Commons 'Map of the Jolof Empire' (15th century), georeferenced on Cap-Vert, Podor and Barra.

regions.name: Jolof Empire
regions.note: Jolof after Sine and Saloum broke away (1520): Jolof, Waalo, Kajoor and Bawol, until Kajoor's victory at Danki (1549) broke up the confederation (it was effectively over by 1600). Approximate. Sources: Wikipedia 'Jolof Empire'; frontiers of the constituent states follow the CC0 Commons 'Map of the Jolof Empire' (15th century), georeferenced on Cap-Vert, Podor and Barra.

regions.name: Kingdom of Jolof
regions.note: The landlocked core left to the Burba after Danki (1549), squeezed between Cayor, Waalo, Futa Toro and Saloum. It became part of French Senegal in 1890. Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Jolof Empire'; frontiers of the constituent states follow the CC0 Commons 'Map of the Jolof Empire' (15th century), georeferenced on Cap-Vert, Podor and Barra.

regions.name: Waalo
regions.note: Wolof kingdom of the lower Senegal valley and delta, ruled by the Brak. Waalo dated its kings from 1287 but was a member of the Jolof confederation until the battle of Danki (1549), after which it paid Jolof only symbolic tribute (to 1715); the French annexed it in 1855. The northern edge is set on the river: the north-bank lands it held at times were shared with the Moorish emirates. Approximate. Sources: Wikipedia 'Waalo'; Wikipedia 'Jolof Empire'; frontiers of the constituent states follow the CC0 Commons 'Map of the Jolof Empire' (15th century), georeferenced on Cap-Vert, Podor and Barra.

regions.name: Cayor

rulers.name: Dece Fu Njogu
rulers.when: Damel who refused tribute to Jolof, 1549

regions.note: The largest Wolof kingdom to break from Jolof (battle of Danki, 1549), between Waalo, Jolof and Baol, including Cap-Vert. Baol was joined to it from 1697 to 1756. Drawn to 1879, when the French began to annex it; Lat Dior fought on until 1886. Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Cayor'; Wikipedia 'Jolof Empire'; frontiers of the constituent states follow the CC0 Commons 'Map of the Jolof Empire' (15th century), georeferenced on Cap-Vert, Podor and Barra.

regions.name: Baol
regions.note: Wolof kingdom of the Teigne between Cayor and Sine, on the Petite Côte; independent of Jolof after Danki (1549), joined to Cayor 1697–1756; France conquered most of it by 1874 and the rest by 1894–95. Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Baol'; Wikipedia 'Jolof Empire'; frontiers of the constituent states follow the CC0 Commons 'Map of the Jolof Empire' (15th century), georeferenced on Cap-Vert, Podor and Barra.

regions.name: Kingdom of Sine

rulers.name: Maad a Sinig Maysa Wali Jaxate Manneh
Maad a Sinig Kumba Ndoffene Famak Joof

regions.note: Serer kingdom of the Maad a Sinig, a member of the Jolof confederation until it broke away in 1520, then independent until it became a French protectorate (1891). Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Sine'; Wikipedia 'Jolof Empire'; frontiers of the constituent states follow the CC0 Commons 'Map of the Jolof Empire' (15th century), georeferenced on Cap-Vert, Podor and Barra.

regions.name: Saloum
regions.note: Serer-Wolof kingdom of the Buur Saloum around Kahone, founded c. 1494 and independent of Jolof from 1520; it held Gambia-river chiefdoms (Niumi, Baddibu) as tributaries, which are not drawn. Maba Diakhou Bâ's jihad (1860s) and French expansion ended its independence; drawn to 1891. Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Saloum'; Wikipedia 'Jolof Empire'; frontiers of the constituent states follow the CC0 Commons 'Map of the Jolof Empire' (15th century), georeferenced on Cap-Vert, Podor and Barra.

regions.name: Kaabu
regions.note: Mandinka kingdom of the Upper Guinea coast, Mali's westernmost province until it became independent as Mali declined (c. 1537); it fell when the Futa Jallon Fula stormed Kansala in 1867. The border data's late Mali Empire outline still covers this area in places; Kaabu is drawn on top. Kansala's site and Kaabu's limits toward the Bissagos coast and the Casamance are approximate. Source: Wikipedia 'Kaabu'.

regions.name: Empire of Great Fulo (Denianke kingdom)
regions.note: The Denianke Fula kingdom that Koli Tenguella took from Jolof in 1513, after his father Tenguella's state was destroyed by Songhai (1512); it dominated the middle Senegal valley from the early 16th century. Only the valley is drawn. Ended by the Torodbe revolution (1776). Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Empire of Great Fulo'.

regions.name: Imamate of Futa Toro
regions.note: The Torodbe clerics' imamate that replaced the Denianke in 1776, along the middle Senegal valley. France annexed it in 1859, after decades within the French sphere of influence. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Imamate of Futa Toro'.

regions.name: Bundu

rulers.name: Amadi Gai
rulers.when: from 1764, first to take the title almamy

regions.note: Fula Muslim state between the Falémé and the upper Gambia (about 13–15°N, 12–13°W), founded by the Torodbe cleric Malick Sy in 1690; the most powerful state on the upper Senegal by 1716. It became a French protectorate in the 1850s. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Bundu (state)'.

regions.name: Imamate of Futa Jallon
regions.note: Fula theocracy of the Futa Jallon highlands, created by the jihad of 1725 and governed by alternating Almamys at Timbo with provincial diwals (Labé the largest). French conquest 1896. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Imamate of Futa Jallon'.

regions.name: Emirate of Trarza
regions.note: Moorish (Hassaniya) emirate of south-western Mauritania, north of the lower Senegal, which dominated the gum trade with Saint-Louis. Nomadic emirates had no fixed frontiers; the outline marks the core grazing lands only. Coppolani's treaties brought it under French protection in 1902–04. Source: Wikipedia 'Emirate of Trarza'.

regions.name: Emirate of Brakna
regions.note: Moorish emirate of the Awlad Abdullah (Brakna), independent of the other Beni Hassan from 1674, east of Trarza, north of Futa Toro on the middle Senegal. Nomadic: the outline marks core lands only, very approximately. French protectorate 1903. Source: Wikipedia 'Emirate of Brakna'.

regions.name: Kaarta
regions.note: Bambara kingdom of the Massassi Coulibaly, rival to Ségou, in the Sahel of western Mali; an earlier Kaarta (from c. 1635) was destroyed by Ségou in 1754 and re-founded the same year. El Hadj Umar Tall took its capital Nioro in 1855. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Kaarta'.

regions.name: Toucouleur Empire
regions.note: El Hadj Umar Tall's state after he took Nioro, the capital of Kaarta (1855), with Bambuk and Dinguiraye to the south-west (not drawn). The French checked him at Médine (1857); the treaty of 1860 left him Kaarta and Ségou. Approximate. Source: Wikipedia 'Tukulor Empire'.

regions.name: Toucouleur Empire
regions.note: The state El Hadj Umar Tall built by jihad: Kaarta (1855), Ségou (1861) and Massina (1862). His successors split it between Ahmadu at Ségou, Tijani at Bandiagara and governors at Nioro. Drawn until the French took Ségou in 1890 (Nioro fell in 1891, Bandiagara in 1893). Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Tukulor Empire'.

regions.name: Samorian State (Wassoulou Empire)
regions.note: Samori Ture's Mandinka state on the upper Niger and Milo, at its widest in the 1880s. Its frontiers moved with his armies; the outline is approximate. Source: Wikipedia 'Samorian State'.

regions.name: Samorian State (Wassoulou Empire)
regions.note: Driven east by the French, Samori rebuilt his state in northern Côte d'Ivoire and western Ghana (Dabakala, Bouna) from 1892 until his capture in 1898. Very approximate. Source: Wikipedia 'Samorian State'.

regions.name: Kénédougou Kingdom
regions.note: Senufo-Dyula kingdom of the Traoré around Sikasso; the dynasty is traced to the 17th century, but the kingdom grew large only from the 1820s. It resisted Samori (siege of Sikasso, 1887–88) and fell to the French in 1898. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Kénédougou Kingdom'.

regions.name: Kong Empire
regions.note: Dyula trading state of the Wattara at Kong, at its widest under Seku Wattara, who extended it north toward Bobo-Dioulasso and the Black Volta. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Kong Empire'.

regions.name: Kong Empire
regions.note: After Seku Wattara's death (1745) the northern conquests broke away (Gwiriko at Bobo-Dioulasso) and Kong remained a smaller merchant state; Binger signed agreements there in 1888, and Samori burned it in 1897 (or 1898). Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Kong Empire'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Wogodogo (Mossi)
regions.note: The largest Mossi kingdom, ruled by the Mogho Naba at Ouagadougou. Traditional dates put its founder Oubri in the 11th–12th century; many scholars prefer c. 1495, used here. Askia Muhammad of Songhai warred on the Mossi in 1497. France took the kingdom in 1896. Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Mossi Kingdoms', 'List of rulers of Wogodogo'.

regions.name: Yatenga
regions.note: Northern Mossi kingdom; Naaba Kango founded Ouahigouya as its capital. Founding date traditional; French protectorate 1895. Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Mossi Kingdoms', 'Yatenga Province'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Dagbon
regions.note: Dagomba kingdom of northern Ghana; the capital moved east to Yendi after wars with Gonja c. 1700. Tributary to Asante from 1744 to 1874 but self-governing; Germans destroyed Yendi at Adibo in 1896, and the kingdom was divided between German Togo and the British Gold Coast. Founding date traditional; approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Dagbon'.

regions.name: Gonja

rulers.name: Sumaila Ndewura Jakpa
rulers.when: 17th c., founder of the Yagbongwura line

regions.note: Kingdom of the Mande Ngbanya between the Black and White Volta, under a paramount chief (Yagbongwura) by 1675. Asante conquered it in 1751–52; the border data's Asante outline covers its southern part from 1744, so it is drawn to 1743. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Gonja'.

regions.name: Denkyira
regions.note: Akan gold state of south-western Ghana that dominated the Gold Coast hinterland until its defeat by Asante at Feyiase (1701). Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Denkyira'.

regions.name: Akwamu
regions.note: Akan kingdom in the hills north of Accra (Atewa hills), first recorded on a Dutch map of 1629, before its conquest of the coast. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Akwamu'.

regions.name: Akwamu
regions.note: After taking Accra (1677–81) and Ladoku (1679) Akwamu ruled the coast from the Accra plains to the Volta, and crossed it in 1702; Akyem and its allies destroyed it in 1730. Only the lasting core is drawn; approximate. Source: Wikipedia 'Akwamu'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Allada (Ardra)

rulers.name: Kokpon
rulers.when: c. 1600, first king of Great Ardra

regions.note: Aja kingdom of the Slave Coast, the 'Great Ardra' of European sources, with its ports at Offra and Jakin. It paid tribute to Oyo. Conquered by Dahomey in 1724. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Ardra'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Whydah
regions.note: Hueda kingdom on the coast around Ouidah and Savi, the busiest slave port of the Bight of Benin c. 1700; it broke from Allada in the mid-17th century and fell to Dahomey in 1727. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Whydah'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Dahomey
regions.note: Fon kingdom on the Abomey plateau, inland of Allada, founded around 1600 by an offshoot of Allada's royal line; Houegbadja built the Abomey palaces. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Dahomey'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Dahomey
regions.note: Agaja conquered Allada in 1724; Whydah followed in 1727. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Dahomey'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Dahomey
regions.note: Dahomey held the coast from Ouidah to Cotonou. After wars with Oyo (1728–1740) it paid Oyo tribute until Ghezo stopped it in the 1820s, but ran its own affairs; the border data's Oyo outline covers it in some years and Dahomey is drawn on top. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Dahomey'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Dahomey
regions.note: After Oyo's fall Dahomey expanded north into the Mahi country and toward the Mono. Conquered by France in 1892–94. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Dahomey'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Benin
regions.note: Edo kingdom around Benin City under the Obas of the Eweka dynasty, which replaced the Ogiso rulers of Igodomigodo; the early dates are traditional. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Benin'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Benin
regions.note: Under Ewuare and his successors Benin expanded west toward Lagos, north into Ekiti and Akoko and east to the Niger. The outline keeps to lands under the Oba's governors; tributary areas further out are left off. Approximate. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Benin'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Benin
regions.note: A smaller kingdom after the civil wars of the late 17th century, until the British punitive expedition of 1897. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Benin'.

regions.name: Nupe Kingdom
regions.note: Kingdom of the Etsu Nupe astride the middle Niger above the Kaduna confluence. The kingdom is dated 1531–1835 in Stewart's king-list (Wikipedia gives the mid-15th century for its origins); after Etsu Ma'azu (d. 1818) the Fulani took over, and it became the Bida Emirate within Sokoto, which the border data draws from 1805. Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Bida Emirate'; the CC BY-SA Commons 'Map of western Hausaland in the late 18th century', georeferenced on Birnin Kebbi, Jebba and Zaria.

regions.name: Kingdom of Kano
regions.note: Hausa kingdom around the walled city of Kano, chronicled in the Kano Chronicle from Bagauda (999); Islamised under Yaji (14th c.) and Rumfa. Taken by the Fulani jihad in 1805–07. Approximate frontiers; the early dates are traditional. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Kano'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Katsina

rulers.name: Muhammadu Korau
rulers.when: founder of the Korau dynasty, mid-15th c. (older works: c. 1348)

regions.note: Hausa kingdom and trans-Saharan terminus, established early in the second millennium; Muhammadu Korau founded its best-known dynasty. Taken by the jihad (1805–06); the old dynasty moved to Maradi. Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Katsina'; the CC BY-SA Commons 'Map of western Hausaland in the late 18th century', georeferenced on Birnin Kebbi, Jebba and Zaria.

regions.name: Zazzau
regions.note: Southernmost Hausa kingdom, a slave-raiding frontier state; Amina's campaigns and walls are dated to the late 16th century, though her reign is not in the king-lists. Taken by the jihad in 1808 (the Hausa dynasty moved to Abuja). Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Amina of Zazzau'; the CC BY-SA Commons 'Map of western Hausaland in the late 18th century', georeferenced on Birnin Kebbi, Jebba and Zaria.

regions.name: Gobir
regions.note: Hausa kingdom of the north-west, tributary to Bornu until Bawa (1777) and to Kebbi before c. 1715. Gobir lay in the Sahel of today's Niger (Birnin Lalle) in this period. The jihad of Usman dan Fodio began in Gobir (1804); Alkalawa fell in 1808. Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Gobir'; the CC BY-SA Commons 'Map of western Hausaland in the late 18th century', georeferenced on Birnin Kebbi, Jebba and Zaria.

regions.name: Gobir
regions.note: Hausa kingdom of the north-west, tributary to Bornu until Bawa (1777) and to Kebbi before c. 1715. Under pressure from the Tuareg, Gobir moved south toward the Rima valley. The jihad of Usman dan Fodio began in Gobir (1804); Alkalawa fell in 1808. Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Gobir'; the CC BY-SA Commons 'Map of western Hausaland in the late 18th century', georeferenced on Birnin Kebbi, Jebba and Zaria.

regions.name: Gobir
regions.note: Hausa kingdom of the north-west, tributary to Bornu until Bawa (1777) and to Kebbi before c. 1715. Babari destroyed Birnin Zamfara (c. 1756 or 1762) and ruled from Alkalawa on the Rima. The jihad of Usman dan Fodio began in Gobir (1804); Alkalawa fell in 1808. Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Gobir'; the CC BY-SA Commons 'Map of western Hausaland in the late 18th century', georeferenced on Birnin Kebbi, Jebba and Zaria.

regions.name: Kingdom of Zamfara

rulers.name: Mairoki
rulers.when: besieged by Bawa of Gobir, late 18th c.

regions.note: Hausa kingdom between Kebbi, Gobir and Katsina, centred first on Dutsi. A tributary of Kebbi until it revolted c. 1715 (drawn from then); it lost its northern lands and its capital to Gobir c. 1756–62 and was absorbed by the jihad c. 1805. Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Zamfara'; the CC BY-SA Commons 'Map of western Hausaland in the late 18th century', georeferenced on Birnin Kebbi, Jebba and Zaria.

regions.name: Kingdom of Zamfara

rulers.name: Mairoki
rulers.when: besieged by Bawa of Gobir, late 18th c.

regions.note: Hausa kingdom between Kebbi, Gobir and Katsina, centred first on Dutsi. A tributary of Kebbi until it revolted c. 1715 (drawn from then); it lost its northern lands and its capital to Gobir c. 1756–62 and was absorbed by the jihad c. 1805. Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Zamfara'; the CC BY-SA Commons 'Map of western Hausaland in the late 18th century', georeferenced on Birnin Kebbi, Jebba and Zaria.

regions.name: Kingdom of Kebbi
regions.note: Kanta Kuta of Leka broke from Songhai in 1516–17, and under Muhammad Kanta Kebbi became the leading power of western Hausaland, taking tribute from the Hausa states (which stopped after 1556) and holding Zamfara and Gobir as tributaries until c. 1715. Only the Kebbi-Rima core is drawn; the border data's Songhai outline may overlap it before 1591. Approximate. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Kebbi'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Kebbi
regions.note: A reduced Kebbi along the Kebbi river after Zamfara and Gobir revolted (c. 1715), until the jihad defeated it (1805–08); the dynasty survived at Argungu. Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Kebbi'; the CC BY-SA Commons 'Map of western Hausaland in the late 18th century', georeferenced on Birnin Kebbi, Jebba and Zaria.

regions.name: Gao Empire (Kingdom of Gao)
regions.note: The Songhai kingdom of Gao on the Niger bend, known to Arab geographers from the 9th century and from royal epitaphs from 1042. Mali brought Gao under its rule around 1300 (dates range from the late 13th century to Mansa Musa in 1324); the border data's Mali outline already covers Gao from the 1230s, and Gao is drawn on top of it until 1299. Only the river valley is drawn; dates and extent are uncertain. Later imperial Songhai (from 1464) is in the border data. Source: Wikipedia 'Gao Empire'.

regions.name: Dendi Kingdom
regions.note: The free Songhai kingdom of the Askias in the lower Niger valley after the Moroccan conquest of Gao (1591); the border data draws Songhai to 1608. In the later 17th century its north broke into separate Songhay chiefdoms. Approximate. Source: Wikipedia 'Dendi (province)'.

regions.name: Dendi Kingdom
regions.note: The Askia kingdom of Dendi proper, on the Niger around Gaya, after the northern Songhay chiefdoms went their own way. The French deposed the last askia in 1901; drawn to 1898. Approximate. Source: Wikipedia 'Dendi (province)'.

regions.name: Sultanate of Agadez

rulers.name: Akkasan
rulers.when: his successor, moved the seat to Agadez

regions.note: Tuareg sultanate of Aïr, founded c. 1405 according to oral history (other works give 1449), with its seat at Agadez soon after the town's founding (1413); conquered by Songhai in 1500 and independent again after 1591. French rule from 1906; drawn to 1899. The outline is the Aïr massif and its edges; Tuareg confederations ranged far beyond it. Very approximate. Source: Wikipedia 'Sultanate of Agadez'.

regions.name: Sultanate of Damagaram
regions.note: Sultanate founded in 1731 near Mirriah by Muslim Kanuri aristocrats, at first a vassal of Bornu; it absorbed Bornu's other western vassals and made Zinder its capital. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Sultanate of Damagaram'.

regions.name: Sultanate of Damagaram
regions.note: In the 19th century Damagaram absorbed some 18 Bornu vassal states and was effectively independent; the Voulet–Chanoine column took Zinder in 1899. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Sultanate of Damagaram'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Baguirmi
regions.note: Sultanate on the Chari south-east of Lake Chad. It was a tributary of Bornu for much of its history (fully independent in the 18th century), was conquered by Wadai in 1805 and by Rabih az-Zubayr in 1893, but kept its own mbang; the border data's Bornu outline covers it in some years and Baguirmi is drawn on top. French protectorate 1897. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Baguirmi'.

regions.name: Mauro-Roman Kingdom

rulers.name: Masuna
rulers.when: 'king of the Moors and Romans', Altava inscription of 508

regions.note: Berber-Roman kingdom of western Mauretania (Oranie), known from the Altava inscription of 508 naming Masuna 'rex gentium Maurorum et Romanorum', and from Procopius. The inscription names officials Masuna appointed at Altava and two other towns. It took shape as Roman rule ended in Mauretania Caesariensis (the Vandals invaded Africa in 429), and Garmul, whom some historians count as a later king, was killed by the Byzantines in 578. Scholars disagree on how far it was a single kingdom and how large it was (‘much of Mauretania Caesariensis’ in some accounts); the outline is a conservative guess around Altava, Tlemcen and the lower Chelif. The border data's Vandal outline overlaps its eastern edge. Source: Wikipedia 'Mauro-Roman Kingdom'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Altava
regions.note: The smaller romanised Berber kingdom ruled from Altava after Garmul's defeat (578). Its last recorded ruler Kusaila ambushed and killed Uqba ibn Nafi near Biskra (683) and drove the Arabs from Kairouan; he died in 688. The end date is uncertain. The border data's Umayyad outline covers the area from the 680s; Altava is drawn on top of it. Drawn conservatively. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Altava'.

regions.name: Kingdom of the Aurès
regions.note: Christian Berber kingdom of the Aurès massif, founded in the 480s by Masties after revolts against the Vandals (his inscription of c. 516 calls him dux and imperator). Its last queen, Dihya, led the resistance to the Arabs until she was killed in 703. Its reach beyond the mountains varied; the outline keeps to the massif and its piedmont, and is drawn on top of the border data's Umayyad outline in the 680s–700s. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of the Aurès'.

regions.name: Sultanate of Tuggurt

rulers.name: Yusuf ibn Hasan
rulers.when: chief, made to submit by the Hafsids in 1449 and 1465

regions.note: Oasis sultanate of the Berber Banu Jallab over Touggourt and the Oued Righ from the 15th century; Hafsid Tunis and later Ottoman Algiers (Salah Rais's expedition of 1552) imposed tribute at times, but it kept its own sultans. The French took Touggourt in 1854 (the sultanate is dated to 1881 in some accounts). Drawn as the Oued Righ oases, approximately. Source: Wikipedia 'Sultanate of Tuggurt'.

regions.name: Sultanate of Shewa
regions.note: Muslim sultanate of the Makhzumi dynasty in the eastern Shewa lowlands. Its founding date (AH 283, 896 CE) rests on a single retrospective entry in the Chronicle of Shewa; the Walashma of Ifat deposed the dynasty in 1285. Dates and extent are very uncertain, and the border data's Ethiopian outline overlaps it in 1272–84. Source: Wikipedia 'Sultanate of Shewa'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Damot
regions.note: Kingdom south of the Abay (Blue Nile), possibly formed in the 10th century and powerful by the 13th, when it forced the Sultanate of Shewa to pay tribute; Amda Seyon conquered it in 1316–17. Its location is placed south of the Abay following most historians; the outline is very approximate. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Damot'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Kaffa
regions.note: Highland kingdom bounded on the north by the Gojeb river, founded c. 1390 according to tradition. From the late 17th century it annexed neighbouring Gimira states and reached the Omo under Tato Shagi Sherocho; only the core is drawn. Menelik II's armies conquered it in 1897. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Kaffa'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Jimma
regions.note: The largest of the Oromo Gibe kingdoms, which emerged in the 18th century as a rich Muslim market state. Abba Jifar II submitted to Menelik in 1882–84 and kept autonomy until 1932; drawn to 1884. Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Jimma'; positions follow the CC BY-SA Commons map 'Gibe kingdoms'.

regions.name: Limmu-Ennarea
regions.note: Oromo Gibe kingdom on the old lands of Ennarea, the leading Gibe state under Abba Bagibo. Conquered by Shewa in 1891. Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Limmu-Ennarea'; positions follow the CC BY-SA Commons map 'Gibe kingdoms'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Gomma

rulers.name: Abba Boke
rulers.when: first king (or his son Abba Manno)

regions.note: Small Oromo Gibe kingdom around Agaro, emerging in the 18th century, wholly Muslim by 1841; Beshua Abue conquered it for Menelik II in 1886. Approximate. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Gomma'; positions follow the CC BY-SA Commons map 'Gibe kingdoms'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Gumma

rulers.name: Firisa
rulers.when: son of the last king, resisted until 1902

regions.note: Oromo Gibe kingdom west of Gomma, bounded on the east by the bend of the Didessa; its dynasty took power around 1770. Menelik II conquered it in 1885. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Gumma'; positions follow the CC BY-SA Commons map 'Gibe kingdoms'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Gera
regions.note: The last Gibe kingdom to form, founded c. 1835 between Gomma and Kaffa; Dejazmach Besha Abua conquered it in 1887. Approximate. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Gera'; positions follow the CC BY-SA Commons map 'Gibe kingdoms'.

regions.name: Sultanate of Aussa
regions.note: Afar sultanate of the Mudaito dynasty in the lower Awash basin. The border data's Ethiopian Empire outline covers the area; Aussa was outside the emperors' control until it accepted Menelik's overlordship in the 1890s (it stayed autonomous until 1936). Drawn to 1895, on top of that outline. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Sultanate of Aussa'.

regions.name: Shilluk Kingdom
regions.note: Kingdom of the Shilluk reth on the left (west) bank of the White Nile, founded in 1490 according to Shilluk tradition; from Odak Ochollo's reign to 1861 it pushed its northern border down the Nile. Egyptian and trader incursions ended its independence in the 1860s. Approximate frontiers; founding date traditional. Source: Wikipedia 'Shilluk Kingdom'.

regions.name: Warsangali Sultanate
regions.note: Somali state of the Warsangali in Maakhir (Sanaag) on the Gulf of Aden coast, consolidated by Garaad Abdulle Mahmud I from 1613 (older traditions give 1218). British protectorate treaty 1886; the state lasted until 1920. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Warsangali Sultanate'.

regions.name: Sultanate of Mogadishu
regions.note: City-state sultanate that ruled Mogadishu and its Benadir hinterland, founded in the mid-13th century (or 1330 in some accounts); Ibn Battuta found it at its zenith in 1331. Drawn to 1499; in the 16th century it was within the Ajuran sphere. Approximate. Source: Wikipedia 'Sultanate of Mogadishu'.

regions.name: Ajuran Sultanate
regions.note: Somali sultanate of the Garen imams that controlled the Shabelle and Jubba lands and the Benadir ports in the 16th–17th centuries, resisting Portuguese and Oromo pressure until it collapsed in the late 17th century. Its earlier history (from the 13th century) is too poorly known to draw. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Ajuran Sultanate'.

regions.name: Geledi Sultanate
regions.note: Somali sultanate of the Gobroon dynasty on the lower Shabelle (from the late 17th century), which dominated the Benadir hinterland in the 19th century. Italian treaties from 1889; incorporated into Italian Somaliland in 1911. The border data's Omani (Zanzibar) coast outline overlaps it around 1850. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Geledi Sultanate'.

regions.name: Kilwa Sultanate

rulers.name: Ibrahim
rulers.when: emir when the Portuguese took Kilwa, 1505

regions.note: Swahili city-state on Kilwa island, whose history begins c. 960–1000. A sultan of 1178–1195 took Sofala from the Mogadishans, and at its height Kilwa's authority reached along the whole Swahili coast; only the island, Mafia and the adjacent mainland coast it ruled directly are drawn. The Portuguese took Kilwa in 1505. Source: Wikipedia 'Kilwa Sultanate'.

regions.name: Pate Sultanate
regions.note: Swahili sultanate of the Nabhani on Pate island, which ruled the Lamu archipelago and nearby mainland at its height in the 17th–18th centuries. The Pate Chronicle dates the Nabhani to 1203; the chronology is traditional, so the region starts at 1300. Drawn until Lamu's victory at Shela (1813), after which Oman dominated; the dynasty moved to Witu in 1858. Approximate. Source: Wikipedia 'Pate Island'.

regions.name: Buganda
regions.note: Kingdom of the Kabaka on the north-west shore of Lake Victoria, small in this period beside Bunyoro. Dates come from king-lists and are approximate; frontiers approximate. Sources: Wikipedia; positions checked against the CC BY-SA Commons map 'Great Lakes Kingdoms' ('Buganda').

regions.name: Buganda
regions.note: Buganda grew at Bunyoro's expense in the 18th century (Buddu, Singo, Kooki's overlordship) into the strongest lake state. British protectorate 1894. Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia; positions checked against the CC BY-SA Commons map 'Great Lakes Kingdoms' ('Buganda').

regions.name: Bunyoro (Bunyoro-Kitara)
regions.note: Kingdom of the Babiito Omukama, the dominant lake state of the 16th–17th centuries, here including Toro. Its raids reached far wider than the area drawn. Approximate frontiers; early dates traditional. Sources: Wikipedia; positions checked against the CC BY-SA Commons map 'Great Lakes Kingdoms' ('Bunyoro').

regions.name: Bunyoro (Bunyoro-Kitara)
regions.note: Bunyoro after Toro broke away (c. 1830), until Kabalega's defeat and capture by the British (1899). Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia; positions checked against the CC BY-SA Commons map 'Great Lakes Kingdoms' ('Bunyoro').

regions.name: Ankole (Nkore)
regions.note: Kingdom of the Omugabe in south-western Uganda, east of Lake Edward, dated from the 15th century; it was incorporated into the Uganda Protectorate by the Ankole Agreement of 1901. Drawn to 1899, since the border data's British outline covers it from 1900. Approximate frontiers; early dates traditional. Sources: Wikipedia; positions checked against the CC BY-SA Commons map 'Great Lakes Kingdoms' ('Ankole').

regions.name: Karagwe
regions.note: Highland kingdom between Rwanda and Lake Victoria, founded around 1450 according to its king-list; at its height under Rumanyika, a hub of the caravan trade (visited by Speke and Grant, 1861). German rule from 1890. Approximate frontiers; early dates traditional. Sources: Wikipedia; positions checked against the CC BY-SA Commons map 'Great Lakes Kingdoms' ('Karagwe').

regions.name: Kingdom of Rwanda
regions.note: Kingdom of the Mwami in central Rwanda; early reigns are dated from king-lists and are uncertain. Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia; positions checked against the CC BY-SA Commons map 'Great Lakes Kingdoms' ('Kingdom of Rwanda').

regions.name: Kingdom of Rwanda
regions.note: Rwanda expanded to roughly its modern limits under Rwabugiri; German protectorate from 1897. Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia; positions checked against the CC BY-SA Commons map 'Great Lakes Kingdoms' ('Kingdom of Rwanda').

regions.name: Kingdom of Burundi
regions.note: Kingdom of the Mwami, created in the 16th century; Ntare I unified its two centres (the accepted founding date is 1680). Dates from king-lists; approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia; positions checked against the CC BY-SA Commons map 'Great Lakes Kingdoms' ('Kingdom of Burundi').

regions.name: Kingdom of Burundi
regions.note: Ntare Rugamba's conquests gave Burundi roughly its modern extent by 1850. Assigned to German East Africa in 1890 but not effectively occupied (a German post from 1896, treaty of Kiganda 1903); drawn to 1899, since the border data's German outline covers it from 1900. Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia; positions checked against the CC BY-SA Commons map 'Great Lakes Kingdoms' ('Kingdom of Burundi').

regions.name: Kingdom of Loango
regions.note: Vili kingdom on the coast north of the Congo mouth, first mentioned c. 1561 and probably founded by Njimbe c. 1565, once a vassal of Kongo; an independent trading power until French treaties in 1883. Its northern limit toward Mayumba is uncertain. Approximate. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Loango'; the CC BY-SA Commons map 'Kongo 1648' (J. Thornton), georeferenced on its printed graticule.

regions.name: Kingdom of Ndongo
regions.note: Mbundu kingdom in the highlands between the Lukala and the Kwanza; its ruler's title, ngola, gave Angola its name. Listed among Kongo's dependencies in 1535, it is usually taken to be independent after its war with Kongo c. 1556. Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Ndongo'; the CC BY-SA Commons map 'Kongo 1648' (J. Thornton), georeferenced on its printed graticule.

regions.name: Kingdom of Ndongo
regions.note: Ndongo after the Portuguese of Luanda (1576) took the lower Kwanza and Massangano (1583). Nzinga withdrew east to Matamba after 1626. Approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Ndongo'; the CC BY-SA Commons map 'Kongo 1648' (J. Thornton), georeferenced on its printed graticule.

regions.name: Kingdom of Matamba
regions.note: Queen Njinga took Matamba in 1631 and ruled it with the remnant of Ndongo as an independent kingdom; it accepted Portuguese overlordship after the war of 1744. Extent follows the grey area of the CC BY-SA Commons map 'Kongo 1648' (J. Thornton), georeferenced on its printed graticule; approximate. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Matamba'.

regions.name: Kasanje Kingdom

rulers.name: Kasanje
rulers.when: Imbangala leader who gave the state its name, c. 1620

regions.note: Imbangala kingdom formed in 1620 by a band that deserted the Portuguese, in the Baixa de Kasanje west of the Kwango; middleman in the slave trade between Lunda and Luanda (some 300,000 people in 1680). Portugal incorporated it in 1910–11; it is drawn on top of the border data's Portuguese outline after 1885. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Kasanje Kingdom'.

regions.name: Kuba Kingdom
regions.note: Kingdom of the Kuba (Bushoong) between the Sankuru, Lulua and Kasai, united by Shyaam c. 1625; famous for its court art; Congo Free State forces sacked the capital in 1900. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Kuba Kingdom'.

regions.name: Luba Empire

rulers.name: Kalala Ilunga
rulers.when: traditional founder of the second dynasty

regions.note: Kingdom of the Mulopwe in the Upemba depression and the Lomami-Lualaba lands. Dates come from oral traditions and are uncertain; approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Luba Empire'; the public-domain Commons 'Map sketches of the development of the Luba-Lunda Empire'.

regions.name: Luba Empire
regions.note: Luba expanded greatly between 1700 and 1860, at its widest under Kumwimba Ngombe and Ilunga Kabale; succession wars and slave traders from the east weakened it, and a dispute split it in two in 1889. Tributary areas at the edges are left off. Approximate. Sources: Wikipedia 'Luba Empire'; the public-domain Commons 'Map sketches of the development of the Luba-Lunda Empire'.

regions.name: Lunda Empire
regions.note: Commonwealth of the Mwaant Yaav centred on Musumba in southern Katanga, which controlled some 150,000 km² by 1680. (The border data's 'Kingdom of Lunda' polygon is really Kongo and is relabelled so on this map.) Early dates are traditional; approximate frontiers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Lunda Empire'; the public-domain Commons 'Map sketches of the development of the Luba-Lunda Empire'.

regions.name: Lunda Empire
regions.note: Lunda at its height ruled from the Kwango to the Lualaba; Kazembe, Kasanje's trade partners and the Yaka paid tribute and are not included. Chokwe invaders sacked Musumba in 1887. Approximate. Sources: Wikipedia 'Lunda Empire'; the public-domain Commons 'Map sketches of the development of the Luba-Lunda Empire'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Kazembe
regions.note: Eastern Lunda kingdom founded c. 1740 in the Luapula valley; nominally tributary to the Mwaant Yaav but an independent power, visited by Portuguese expeditions (1796–1831) and Livingstone (1867). Msiri's Yeke state took its western lands from the 1850s. British South Africa Company rule from the 1890s. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Kazembe'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Mapungubwe
regions.note: Early state of the Limpopo-Shashe confluence, known from archaeology: the K2 settlement from c. 1000, then the elite on Mapungubwe hill from c. 1220 (capital of some 5,000 by 1250, a state of perhaps 30,000 km²). It declined as trade moved north to Great Zimbabwe around 1300. Extent inferred from its sites; very approximate. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Mapungubwe'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Zimbabwe
regions.note: The Shona state centred on Great Zimbabwe, an important trade centre by 1250 that replaced Mapungubwe around 1300 and exported gold through the Swahili cities; the city was largely abandoned by the mid-15th century. Known from archaeology; the extent follows zimbabwe-type stone enclosures and is very approximate. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Zimbabwe'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Mutapa
regions.note: Shona kingdom of the Mwenemutapa on the northern Zimbabwe plateau and the Zambezi valley, the 'Monomotapa' of Portuguese sources. Its claimed overlordship over the eastern lowlands is left off. Portuguese vassalage from 1629. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Mutapa'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Mutapa
regions.note: A reduced Mutapa, a Portuguese vassal from 1629 and squeezed by the Rozvi from the 1690s; it withdrew to the Zambezi valley after the mid-18th century. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Mutapa'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Butua (Torwa)
regions.note: Kalanga (western Shona) kingdom of the Torwa dynasty on the south-western plateau, centred on Khami (c. 1425–1683), first recorded by Ahmad ibn Majid in 1502 and famed for its gold; conquered by Changamire Dombo around 1683. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Butua'.

regions.name: Rozvi Empire
regions.note: Shona state of the Changamire Rozvi that conquered Butua, drove the Portuguese from the plateau (1693–95) and dominated most of today's Zimbabwe. Nguni invasions of the 1830s ended it as a state (drawn to 1834); a remnant under Tohwechipi held out until 1866. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Rozvi Empire'.

regions.name: Mthwakazi (Ndebele kingdom)
regions.note: Kingdom founded by Mzilikazi's Northern Ndebele, who settled between the Sanyati and the Limpopo in 1838–40 after leaving the Transvaal; it raided the Shona to the east (not drawn). The British South Africa Company invaded it in November 1893. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Mthwakazi'.

regions.name: Maravi
regions.note: Chewa confederacy of the Kalonga in central and southern Malawi, dated from at least the early 15th century. Kalonga Muzura defeated the rival Lundu (1622) and hosted Gaspar Bocarro (1616); Maravi forces reached the Zambezi and the coast (not drawn). In the 18th century it loosened into separate chiefdoms; this slice ends there, at a rough date. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Maravi'.

regions.name: Gaza Empire
regions.note: Nguni state founded by Soshangane in southern Mozambique after the Mfecane, in its first phase on the lower Limpopo; it defeated the rival Nguni chief Nxaba in 1837. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Gaza Empire'.

regions.name: Gaza Empire
regions.note: The Gaza state at its height (1860s), dominating southern Mozambique and south-eastern Zimbabwe between the Limpopo and the Zambezi, apart from Portuguese coastal posts (Inhambane, Delagoa Bay); Portugal captured Gungunhana in 1895. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Gaza Empire'.

regions.name: Mthethwa Paramountcy
regions.note: Nguni paramountcy of the 18th century north of the Mfolozi that Dingiswayo built into a confederacy (c. 1811, including the then minor Zulu); after his death in battle with the Ndwandwe (1817) Shaka absorbed it into the Zulu kingdom, which the border data draws from 1820. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Mthethwa Paramountcy'.

regions.name: Ndwandwe
regions.note: Nguni kingdom of Zwide, with its main capital on Magudu mountain south of the Pongola; it destroyed the Mthethwa (1817–18) and was defeated by Shaka at the Mhlatuze in 1819–20. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Ndwandwe'.

regions.name: Basotho Kingdom
regions.note: Kingdom gathered by Moshoeshoe (king from 1822) at Thaba Bosiu from refugees of the Difaqane, including lowlands west of the Caledon later lost to the Orange Free State; British treaties of 1843 and 1848. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Moshoeshoe I'.

regions.name: Basotho Kingdom
regions.note: Lesotho during the wars with the Orange Free State (1858, 1865–66), until Britain annexed it as Basutoland in 1868. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Moshoeshoe I'.

regions.name: Lozi Kingdom (Barotseland)
regions.note: Kingdom of the Litunga on the Barotse floodplain of the upper Zambezi. Dates traditional; approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Lozi kingdom'.

regions.name: Kololo Kingdom
regions.note: Sotho-speaking Kololo under Sebetwane conquered the Lozi c. 1840 and ruled the upper Zambezi from Linyanti (where Livingstone met them) until a Lozi rising in 1864. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Lozi kingdom'.

regions.name: Lozi Kingdom (Barotseland)
regions.note: The Lozi kingdom restored by the rising of 1864; Lewanika's concessions (1889–1899) brought it under the British South Africa Company. In the late 19th century its sphere covered some 390,000 km² including tributaries; only the core is drawn. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Lozi kingdom'.

regions.name: Boina Kingdom
regions.note: Sakalava kingdom of north-west Madagascar founded from Menabe, rich from the Mahajanga trade; Merina armies took Mahajanga in 1824 (the border data's Merina outline covers it from 1824, so it is drawn to 1823); the kingdom was occupied after 1832 and annexed in 1840. Approximate frontiers. Source: Wikipedia 'Boina Kingdom'.

regions.name: Menabe
regions.note: Sakalava kingdom of the Maroseraña dynasty on the west coast of Madagascar, the first Sakalava state, which rose under Andriandahifotsy in the 17th century. Radama I ravaged it in 1820–22; the Merina subjugated its southern lands in 1834 and resistance continued to 1846 and beyond. Drawn to 1823, since the border data's Merina outline covers most of it from 1824. Approximate frontiers; founding date approximate. Source: Wikipedia 'Menabe'.

sites.name: Linguère
sites.what: seat of the Burba of Jolof (approximate)

sites.name: Timbo
sites.what: seat of the Almamys of Futa Jallon

sites.name: Nioro du Sahel
sites.what: capital of Kaarta, then El Hadj Umar's capital (1855)

sites.name: Benin City (Edo)
sites.what: seat of the Oba of Benin

sites.name: Agadez
sites.what: seat of the sultans of Aïr

sites.name: Altava (Ouled Mimoun)
sites.what: seat of Masuna (inscription of 508) and of the later kingdom of Altava

sites.name: Fashoda (Kodok)
sites.what: royal seat of the Shilluk reth

sites.name: Mogadishu
sites.what: capital of the Sultanate of Mogadishu

sites.name: Mengo (Kampala)
sites.what: royal capital of Buganda in the 19th century

sites.name: Musumba
sites.what: capital of the Mwaant Yaav (approximate; it moved)

sites.name: Great Zimbabwe
sites.what: capital of the Kingdom of Zimbabwe
